questions.question: How do ES modules work — import, export, and how do they differ from CommonJS?
questions.title: Es Modules
questions.direct_answer: ES modules (ESM) are the standard: export const/function at source, `import { x } from './file'` at consumer. Key semantics: imports are live read-only views of the export binding (a live connection, not a copy); modules are singleton instances evaluated once, cached by URL/path; imports are hoisted and can be used before the import statement; ESM loads asynchronously and parses imports statically before execution. CommonJS (require): synchronous, copies values at require-time, dynamic paths allowed, designed for servers.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P[parse: static imports read] --> L[load: graph fetched, exports linked]
    L --> E[evaluate: bodies run, deps first, once]
    E --> C[cached: same module = same instance]
    subgraph vs-CJS
        R[require: sync, copies, dynamic path]
    end
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The three-phase ESM pipeline (the mechanism worth knowing): PARSE — the module record is built, imports/exports read statically (this is why imports can't be conditional or in try/catch); INSTANTIATE/LOAD — the module graph is walked, each dependency fetched, exports linked as memory cells BEFORE any code runs (this is why circular imports partially work — both modules see each other's bindings, though values may be in TDZ at access time); EVALUATE — module bodies run topologically (dependencies first), once, and the result is cached by specifier — the second import of the same path is the SAME instance (singletons by construction).

Circular-dependency behavior (the classic probe): ESM handles cycles better than CommonJS (which returns a partial exports object mid-require) — but not perfectly: a circularly-imported binding accessed during module EVALUATION may throw TDZ ReferenceError; accessed after evaluation completes, it's fine. The engineering takeaway: cycles are a design smell — extract the shared piece into a third module — but the failure modes are worth being able to name.

The browser/Node split history (the context that explains current weirdness): browsers shipped ESM via <script type=module>; Node spent years on ESM/CJS interop because require's synchronous copy semantics can't be emulated in an async static system — hence the dual-package hazard (a library shipping both forms can give you two singletons), the .mjs/.cjs split, and the createRequire escape hatch for ESM needing to require CJS. Knowing why the rift existed (dynamic-sync vs static-async) is the depth marker this question is really testing.
